item.title: Iran faces 'greatest financial offensive ever', says US treasury secretary
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0qxew81y83o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Iran faces 'greatest financial offensive ever', says US treasury secretary - Published The US has announced a host of sanctions against Iran and its supporters as part of what Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said was "the single greatest financial offensive ever". Labelling it an "economic D-Day" for Iran, Bessent said the US would sever all economic ties with the country and added that any nation financially partnering with Iran would also be isolated. "Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," he told a press conference. Iran has warned it would shut down all oil exports from the region if the war with the US and Israel continues. The Iranian regime has also issued a new warning to shipping to not pass through the Strait of Hormuz without its permission, according to Reuters. One fifth of the world's oil and gas usually passes through strait, a narrow waterway south of Iran, but the flow has been effectively blocked by the country since the conflict began at the end of February, leading to higher oil prices globally. At a press conference on Monday outlining what has been called "Operation Economic Outcast", Bessent said the US was launching an "economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe". "Iran now faces a very clear choice with only two paths before them: complete global isolation....or a path back to normalcy with an opportunity to rejoin the global economy," he said. The treasury secretary added America was "no longer managing the Iranian threat, we are ending it". Bessent said the Treasury Department had mapped networks, facilitators and financial channels used by Iran to evade sanctions to trade oil. The department said it has issued determinations against five sectors: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. The Treasury has also imposed sanctions on almost 60 entities, individuals and vessels. However, the latest threat to the Iranian regime follows several U-turns and extended deadlines from US President Donald Trump's administration in its efforts to end the conflict. Over the course of the war, previous threats have included Trump saying in April that "a whole civilisation will die tonight" unless Iran agreed a deal to end the war and unblock the Strait of Hormuz. The US eventually climbed down from that position after mediator Pakistan intervened and called for more diplomacy. The economic impact of the Iran war is being felt in the US and across the world. Higher oil prices have fuelled concerns over the cost of living, with petrol and diesel prices much higher than they were a year ago. In the US, gasoline prices have surpassed $4 a gallon and affordability is among the top concerns of American voters ahead of the mid-term elections in November. On Monday, a barrel of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil prices, was $93. Last week, Bessent announced the US government would intervene in the bond markets and buy back more government debt in a bid to boost demand for bonds and lower borrowing rates. But the impact of the announcenment was short-lived, with long-term borrowing costs bouncing back up a day later. - Iran nuclear deal: What it all means - Published23 November 2021 - How much could Trump's 'economic D-Day' hurt Iran? - Published3 days ago The Iranian regime already faces tough economic sanctions from the US. Former US president Barack Obama and several US allies had agreed a deal with the country in 2015 which lifted many sanctions in return for Iran agreeing to limit its nuclear programme. However, Trump pulled out of that deal in 2018, calling it "defective at its core, and reimposed all US sanctions on Iran. During Joe Biden's term as US president, he made some attempts to reinstate the Obama-era deal, but this did not happen. In April this year, the Trump administration launched a wave of sanctions on foreign banks and firms doing business with Tehran after it became clear its military operations had not caused Iran's regime to surrender.

item.title: UK PM Burnham vows support for Ukraine despite 'outrageous threats' from Russia
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyqypkrzq5o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Burnham vows support for Ukraine despite 'outrageous threats' from Russia - Published Andy Burnham has promised to keep up the pressure on Russia despite Moscow's "outrageous threats", on his first official visit to Ukraine as UK prime minister. Burnham met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and chaired his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", set up by the UK and France under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer. He said the coalition was "doing everything we can" while urging the US Congress to "ratchet up" economic pressure on Russia. The government has agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile - allowing Ukraine to produce the long-range weapon domestically. - UK missiles offer may help Ukraine - but they are not what Zelensky needs most - Published5 hours ago - Briton fighting for Russia killed in Ukraine - Published2 hours ago Burnham said allies were doing "everything we can" to "dig into our own stocks and help others dig into their stocks" of air defences to protect Ukraine. "This is the moment to keep up the pressure on Russia, the moment to squeeze their ability to fund this illegal war," Burnham said, praising the "strength" of the Ukrainian people. "Ukraine has been Europe's protector, not a drain on our security but the front line in keeping Europe safe." It comes after Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov criticised the UK's decision to share the missile blueprints. Peskov said it prevented "even the slightest progress" towards achieving peace. He told reporters on Monday that the Russian military was already gathering data to locate any missile production sites to destroy them. "Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime. Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire," he added. In response, Burnham said: "Who started the fire? That's the question, isn't it?" He said the issue of missile interceptors would be the main topic at the coalition of the willing meeting. Burnham has been reaffirming the UK's backing for Kyiv in the wake of escalating Russian strikes on Ukraine in recent weeks - including one on a shopping centre on Friday that killed at least 16 people. In a joint statement after the meeting, Burnham and co-chairs French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the group would aim to strength Kyiv's air defences "as a matter or urgent priority". They also condemned Moscow's "systemic and escalating strikes against Ukraine's cities, critical infrastructure and civilians" and pledged to "constrain Russia's war chest through sanctions and actions against the "shadow fleet". The Coalition of the Willing is a partnership of 34 countries including Ukraine. Members met on Monday in either Kyiv or by video conference, with a release stating "leaders once again reaffirmed their commitment to support Ukraine's independence". It came as the European Union said it had released €6.1bn (£5.2bn) in military aid for Ukraine to boost its air defences. The finance is part of a wider €90bn loan from the EU to Ukraine. The UK and Ukraine have also announced a new military technology partnership giving British experts access to Kyiv's Avengers AI Labs database. Downing Street says Ukraine has used sensors and cameras to capture data across the battlefield and it can be used to train AI models "to solve key national security challenges" faced by both countries. On Monday morning the prime minister laid flowers at the graves of Ukrainian soldiers during a service at the National Military Memorial Cemetery. He accepted an award from Zelensky on behalf of the British people recognising the UK's support for Ukraine during an independence day event outside the St Sofia cathedral in Kyiv. In a speech, Burnham compared Ukraine's resistance to Russia to the UK's fight with Nazi Germany, saying: "My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century, you hold that flame in the 21st." In a statement issued ahead of the visit, the prime minister said: "On Ukraine's 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes. "I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine's security is our security." He said the friendship Ukraine shared with the UK would "long outlast Russia's illegal war", adding: "Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace." Moscow earlier warned of "consequences" over the use of British drones by Ukraine in its recent ramping up of strikes on Russian infrastructure. Kyiv has stepped up long-range attacks on Moscow and other Russian regions, targeting oil refineries and warehouses of the country's largest online retailer, Wildberries. The government is allowing UK defence company MBDA to declassify information on its components for the Scalp missile, as Ukraine and France aim to establish assembly lines in Ukraine. Scalp missiles and its UK-produced version, the Storm Shadow, have already been provided to Kyiv by both Britain and France and used to hit military targets inside Russia. Ukraine hopes it can also be given more Patriot interceptor missiles, with Zelensky again asking for more of the weapon, which are used to combat Russia's ballistic missiles. Ukraine has been relying on American supplies of the Patriots, but its stockpiles are running low due to the war in Iran, leaving Ukraine vulnerable to Russian attacks. The Russian embassy in the UK has accused Britain of "deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis", saying "the deeper its involvement in the conflict... the higher the price it will pay". In response, Burnham said last week: "We are not fair-weather friends, we will be there in Ukraine's hour of need and that won't change." Asked on Tuesday about the Russian threat, Burnham maintained the UK was "providing support so that Ukraine can defend itself and that's been the British position all the way through this conflict, by previous prime ministers - it remains the case with me". The visit comes as Russia confirmed its ambassador to the UK, Andrei Kelin, had left his post in London in recent weeks. The Kremlin is yet to put forward a replacement but Russia's embassy to the UK told the BBC it did not reflect an intention to downgrade diplomatic relations between the two nations. Deadly exchanges between Russia and Ukraine continued overnight, with two children killed and seven injured when Ukrainian drone debris hit a private children's centre in Russia, local authorities say. A warehouse belonging to online retailer Ozon was also set on fire, two days after Ukraine said it would target the company for selling dual use items that could be used by the military. It was at the third night in the row that Ozon's warehouses had been targeted, with the company confirming on Saturday that a logistics centre in the Samara region had been hit and a warehouse in Orenburg on Sunday. Three people were also killed in a Russian attack on the north-eastern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv, regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. - UK 'supports Ukraine 100%', Burnham says, after Russia's drone warning - Published6 days ago - UK-made drones strike targets inside Russia - Published16 August Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. item.title: Russia's second-biggest online retailer targeted in Ukrainian strikes
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg598yvrzpro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Russia's second-biggest online retailer targeted in Ukrainian strikes - Published Warehouses belonging to Russia's second-largest online retailer have been hit by a wave of Ukrainian drone strikes. Ozon said its logistics facilities in the southern regions of Krasnodar, Dagestan, Stavropol and Adygea were on fire and several people had been injured following overnight strikes. Ukraine has for weeks struck sites belonging to Wildberries, the country's biggest online retailer, describing the firm as a legitimate target because it supplied components to the military, which Moscow denies. Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Saturday that Ukraine had opened "Pandora's box" by striking economic targets and that Russia would hit back at Kyiv's "most sensitive economic sectors". Russia has targeted Ukraine's civilian infrastructure since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022, and recent Russian attacks have hit Ukrainian warehouses and cargo terminals. Both Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians. Ozon said "a fire broke out" at a logistics centre in Makhachkala, in the southern region of Dagestan, following a drone attack at around 05:00 local time (02:00 GMT) on Monday. The company said earlier that a "major fire" was burning at one of its logistics centres in the city of Krasnodar, 700km (435 miles) to the east of the Dagestan site. Russia's defence ministry said three children had been killed in Krasnodar following a Ukrainian drone attack. Russia's children's rights commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova said they were aged 13, 15 and 16, while six more children had been taken to hospital. - Burnham to hand long-range missile blueprints to Zelensky as he visits Kyiv - Published54 minutes ago Meanwhile, Ozon workers in Adygeysk, in the Adygea region, and Nevinnomyssk, in the Stavropol region, have been evacuated. Videos posted on social media of the Ozon attacks have been verified by the BBC. One shows a drone hitting a warehouse in the Orenburg region, while another shows a large plume of smoke and flames rising from its warehouse in Dagestan. Shares in Ozon fell by as much as 12% on the Moscow Exchange on Monday morning, while shares in its major shareholder, private equity firm AFK Sistema, fell by almost 13%. When asked on Monday whether the Russian government would provide state support to Ozon, the Kremlin said it was "working with business representatives to develop various options for providing support in this difficult situation". The overnight strikes comes a day after Ozon's site in the Samara region was hit. The company said a number of its workers had been injured. Following that strike, Ukraine's defence ministry said on Saturday: "Systematic strikes on dual-use goods storage centres complicate the enemy's logistics and negatively affect the Russian economy as a whole. "After Ukrainian units hit 15 of the largest logistics hubs of Wildberries, it was Ozon's turn." Meanwhile, in Ukraine's Odesa region, overnight strikes targeted food storage facilities and energy infrastructure leading to five people being injured, the region's head Oleg Kiper said on Telegram. Founded in 1998, Ozon is one of Russia's first online retailers. The company is second only to Wildberries in terms of scale and presence, with its pick-up posts and delivery boxes stationed across the country. Both the Ozon and Wildberries logos are often seen together in Russia at shared pick-up points. The targeting of these online retailers has had the effect of bringing the war closer to ordinary Russians. Both companies have been described as "Russia's Amazon" and it is estimated that they are used by 85-90% of Russia's economically active population. In many remote places lacking accessible shops, Russians depend on them for much of their clothes and household appliances. But unlike Amazon, which sells goods directly alongside its marketplace business, Wildberries and Ozon act almost entirely as marketplaces, connecting independent sellers with buyers across Russia, storing and delivering their goods and handling payments. This means many of the losses incurred in the attacks have been borne by those businesses. The Kremlin has denied that online platforms are used for army supplies.

item.title: Israel warns of 'forceful' response to kites flown from Gaza
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y58g2dp3xo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Israel warns of 'forceful' response to kites flown from Gaza - Published Israel has warned Hamas that it will increase strikes on Gaza following concern over launches of kites, drones and balloons from the territory. Several kites were found in an Israeli community near the border with Gaza over the weekend, local media reported. "Forceful actions will be taken to put an end to this phenomenon," Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz said on Monday. Before the war, kites and balloons carrying incendiary devices were launched into Israel, causing fires that burned forest and farmland. Hamas has denied responsibility for the new kites - which were not carrying explosives - and said they belonged to "children searching for their innocent childhood amid the rubble". The group also accused Israel of using the kites as a "pretext" for continued air strikes in Gaza despite the ceasefire agreed last October. - Families' agonising search for answers as thousands still missing in Gaza - Published5 days ago Four kites were found in Kibbutz Nahal Oz, which is about 800m (2,620ft) from the Gaza border, on Friday and Saturday. Several more were found elsewhere in southern Israel last week, according to local media. The Israeli reports cited military sources as saying they believed Hamas was behind the kites and that they might have been intended to test Israel's response. No suspicious materials were attached to the kites and they did not pose a threat, the military said. But Katz warned there would be "zero tolerance" and said: "A balloon is treated like a kite, and a kite is treated like a drone, with or without explosives." Residents of Nahal Oz said in a statement that they feared the return of incendiary kites and balloons, adding: "We will not accept a policy of containment when it comes to our security." Hamas warned of "the danger of the allegations and threats" from Israel and said the kites were "basically children's toys from displacement camps". "These threats are based on fabricated pretexts and are an attempt to justify the continuation of the aggression and violations against our people," a spokesman for the group added. On Sunday, Palestinian health officials said two people were killed and seven others injured in two Israeli strikes in Nuseirat refugee camp and the town of al-Zawayda, both in central Gaza. A four-year-old boy called Mohammed Taha was killed when a building in al-Zawayda, just north of Maghazi refugee camp, was bombed, according to local media. The Israeli military said it killed the commander of a Hamas weapons manufacturing site in the Maghazi area, whom it identified as Ismail Abu Ful, and that it had warned the residents to evacuate beforehand. "There is no ceasefire, there is nothing," Abu Ahmed, a displaced man who had been sheltering nearby, told Reuters news agency. "We want solutions, we want to live in peace." On Monday, Palestinian media reported that a man called Mohammed Abu Asad was killed in an overnight Israeli strike on a tent in the central town of Deir al-Balah. The Israeli military said Abu Asad was a member of the elite Nukhba forces of Hamas's military wing who had taken part in the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack on southern Israel. The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to the cross-border assault, during which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage. More than 74,420 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since then, including 1,288 since the ceasefire took effect, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry.

item.title: King of Norway's health has worsened, palace says
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c36lnekj659o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
King of Norway's health has worsened, palace says - Published King Harald V of Norway's health has worsened, the palace has said, as he remains in hospital receiving antibiotics for a bacterial infection in his bloodstream. The monarch has responded to treatment despite the deterioration in his condition, according to the palace, but he will remain at Oslo University Hospital, Rikshospitalet, and on leave from royal duties until further notice. The 89-year-old, who has been on the throne since 1991, was admitted to hospital and put on sick leave a week ago. His son, Crown Prince Haakon, 53, has been serving as regent while his father is on leave. King Harald has been treated in recent weeks with cortisone for a rare blood condition, haemolytic anaemia. It causes the number of red blood cells in the body to be reduced, and leads to fatigue and shortness of breath. In April 2024, Norway's royal household said that King Harald would make a "permanent reduction" to his public engagements "out of consideration for his age". That year, the king had been fitted with a pacemaker after falling ill on holiday in Malaysia. The Norwegian royal family has already faced a challenging year in 2026. Crown Prince Haakon's wife, Crown Princess Mette-Marit, received a lung transplant in June after she had been diagnosed with a rare form of pulmonary fibrosis in 2018. The transplant came two days after Mette-Marit's son Marius Borg Høiby was sentenced to four years in prison after being convicted of two counts of rape. He had denied the most serious charges and his lawyers said he would appeal the sentence. Høiby, 29, was four when his mother married Crown Prince Haakon and is not himself a royal figure. Also earlier in the year, documents were released revealing Mette-Marit's frequent contact with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. She later apologised to Norway's king and queen for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement", adding in a national TV interview that she wished she had never met him. item.title: Outrage in Nepal over rape and murder of three-year-old girl
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy58ql288o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Outrage in Nepal over rape and murder of three-year-old girl - Published Activists and politicians in Nepal have urged the government to enact tougher laws as the alleged rape and murder of a three-year-old girl has caused outrage across the country. Nepal has seen continued protests since the girl was found dead last week, three days after she went missing in Madhesh province. Nine people have been arrested in connection with the case, a local police spokesman told the BBC. The crime has triggered demands for reform. Police have also been accused of negligence in the initial stages of the investigation after footage of a teenage suspect was leaked onto social media. After days of demonstrations in the city of Simara, the victim's family met government ministers, and secured a written agreement over the weekend. The government has promised to review laws on serious offences, and create a memorial in honour of the child. The incident has also opened a wider debate over how Nepal deals with young offenders, with some campaigners pushing for harsher punishments for minors convicted of rape or murder. Prominent human rights activist Gauri Pradhan called the attack a "very painful incident and the government should punish anyone involved in such atrocious act. There should be some serious efforts for wider reforms". However, he cautioned against calls for the introduction of the death penalty. There has also been anger after a video showing a teenage suspect giving a statement about the suspected murder was uploaded to social media, sparking questions as to how footage of the individual under police custody was leaked. "We have so far found one police personnel directly involved in the [leak] and have initiated action against him," chief district officer of Bara district, Dharmendra Kumar Mishra, told the BBC. "If more officers are found, they will also be punished. We have zero tolerance against such practice." More than 25,500 accusations of rape and sexual abuse were filed between July 2017 to July 2025, according to Nepalese Police. Of these cases, more than 3,200 female victims were under the age of 10, the police say.

item.title: Nearly three million Teslas recalled in China over hidden door handles
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4g6ggdg030o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Nearly three million Teslas recalled in China over hidden door handles - Published Minimalistic door handles became a signature feature of electric vehicles (EVs), but the controversial designs are now at the centre of China's biggest car recall, affecting more than 4 million vehicles. The recall, which includes 2.98 million Chinese-made Teslas, follows safety concerns that the hidden door handles are difficult to locate and open in emergency situations. Other brands affected by the recall include Chinese carmakers XPeng, Xiaomi and Geely. The recalled vehicles will have a warning label stuck on the interior door and receive a software update to automatically lower the windows in a crash. The designs have come under scrutiny after two fatal crashes in China involving Xiaomi EVs, in which power failures were suspected to have prevented doors from being opened. Tesla said in a statement on Friday that it was recalling some of its Model 3, Y, S and X vehicles due to door handles that are "difficult to identify and operate because their colour is similar to the interior trim". "In extreme situations such as a severe collision causing the vehicle's low-voltage system to fail, this could hinder occupants from quickly opening the doors to escape and impede rescue efforts by those outside the vehicle, posing a safety hazard," it said. Tesla said it would place warning labels on the recalled vehicles and issue a software update to automatically lower a vehicle's windows after a collision. It is not clear if the affected firms plan to make a similar recall for the rest of the world. The BBC has contacted Tesla, XPeng, Xiaomi and Geely for comment. The use of hidden handle designs has "snowballed" after Chinese brands were quick to copy the "sleek" look of Tesla's Model S sedan since 2014, said Tu Le, the founder of consultancy Sino Auto Insights. The use of warning labels and a software update is more of a "band-aid" than a lasting solution for the issue, he added. In February, Chinese authorities announced a ban on hidden door handles. Under new rules due to take effect on 1 January 2027, cars will only be allowed to be sold in China if they have a mechanical release on both the inside and outside of their doors. Tesla's door handles were also involved in a probe by US safety regulators after reports that they suddenly stopped working, leaving children trapped in the cars. In July, the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration suggested creating a new formal safety standard for all carmakers. The BBC has contacted the agency for comment. item.title: Sonya Massey's killer Sean Grayson dies in US prison
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgrvj28wrxgo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Sonya Massey's killer Sean Grayson dies in US prison - Published Sean Grayson, the white US police officer convicted of murdering a black woman, Sonya Massey, during an incident at her home in 2024, has died in prison at age 32. Grayson shot dead Massey, 36, during an exchange that took place after she reported a suspected intruder at her residence in Illinois. The killing reignited the debate about police brutality in the US. Grayson said he fired because he thought Massey was about to throw a pot of boiling water on him. He was last year found guilty of second-degree murder. The former police officer was undergoing treatment for colon cancer. His lawyer Daniel Fultz confirmed to the BBC that Grayson had died on Sunday, but did not disclose the cause. The BBC has asked the Illinois Department of Corrections for comment. Lawyers for Massey's family said: "Grayson's death in custody from cancer does not bring Sonya back." "We wish his family prayers of peace, as we do for all who grieve a loved one. Sonya's family knows that pain all too well and will grieve her loss the rest of their days," the lawyers said, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner. Protests took place across the US in the aftermath of Massey's death, and then-President Joe Biden declared that the late woman "should be alive today". - Ex-officer guilty of murder of Sonya Massey after she reported suspected intruder - Published29 October 2025 The incident took place in the early hours over Independence Day weekend in July 2024. Massey called police to her home in Springfield, 200 miles (320km) south of Chicago, to report that she believed someone had broken in to her property. Police bodycam footage of the incident showed the chaotic sequence of events. The shooting happened after an exchange of words about a pot on Massey's stove. Massey and Grayson appeared to laugh over her pot of "steaming hot water", before Massey twice said: "I rebuke you in the name of Jesus." "You better [expletive] not or I swear to God I'll [expletive] shoot you in your [expletive] face," Grayson said. He then drew his pistol as he shouted for her to drop the pot. "OK, I'm sorry," Massey was heard saying before she ducked. Grayson fired three shots, striking her in the face. Grayson, who was subsequently sacked from his job, was charged with first-degree murder, but the jury was allowed to convict him of the lesser charge of second-degree murder. He was sentenced to 20 years in prison. In recent months, he applied for release on medical grounds, but was unsuccessful. He had been diagnosed with cancer in 2023.

item.title: Access to Zambian courts prevented as election petition deadline looms
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgrvjn88rxqo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Zambia courts sealed off as election petition deadline looms - Published Court premises in the Zambian capital, Lusaka, and elsewhere have been shut as the deadline for filing a petition against the outcome of the recent presidential election approaches. An unusual police presence has been reported at some courts, which have been taped off to prevent access. Opposition candidate Brian Mundubile said he would challenge the election result, citing irregularities, after coming second with a 38% share of the vote. Incumbent Hakainde Hichilema won a second term with 60%. Mundubile is in hiding over alleged threats made against him, amid a post-election period marked by controversy, including the shooting dead of an opposition figure and the arrest of others. Monday is the last day on which petition against the presidential election result can be filed. Such a petition could potentially affect the inauguration of Hichilema, which is scheduled for 1 September. On Monday, lawyers who arrived at the courts were being asked to depart. One lawyer told the BBC that three armed men approached his vehicle, identified themselves, and instructed him to leave the area. The courts that have been sealed off include the High Court in Lusaka, the Supreme Court, which also houses the Constitutional Court, and several local courts. It is unclear when the premises will reopen. The BBC has contacted the Zambian police and the judiciary for comment. Local media cite a directive by a judiciary administrative official telling all staff not to report to work following the closure of courts for "security reasons". The memo, which has also been shared online by some opposition figures, does not give details of the security situation. Some commentators have raised concerns over the closure while questioning the independence of the judiciary. A prominent voice for the opposition, Emmanuel Mwamba, alleged the action was aimed at preventing Mundubile from filing his presidential election petition. The Law Association of Zambia (LAZ) said it was concerned by the closure of the courts and the presence of heavily armed military personnel around court premises in Lusaka. It said there was no formal public explanation for the closure nor its expected duration. Referring to the "unsigned memorandum" from the judiciary addressing staff, it said no further official information had been provided to lawyers and the public. "The closure of the courts has immediate implications for access to justice, particularly for persons requiring urgent judicial intervention," it said in a statement It said the timing was "particularly significant in the present electoral context", citing a "seven-day period" in which a person may "petition the Constitutional Court to nullify the election of a President-elect". Despite the court closure, preparations for Hichilema's inauguration appear to be continuing. The youth and sport ministry has issued a media invitation for journalists to accompany a cabinet official on an inspection of arrangements at National Heroes Stadium, where the ceremony is expected to take place. Mundubile last week rejected the presidential election results and said he planned to challenge the outcome through the courts. He remains in a secure location under the protection of what his campaign describes as an "international human rights body". He went into hiding after the arrests of opposition figures and the death of former minister Mutotwe Kafwaya during a raid by security officers, in what officials described as an exchange of fire in a security operation in the capital. The arrests as well as the death of Kafwaya prompted calls from rights groups and the Law Association of Zambia for an independent investigations. Amnesty International described the Kafwaya's killing as "deeply alarming" and called for prompt, thorough and impartial investigations. The lawyers' association similarly expressed "grave concern" and demanded investigation. The election day, 13 August, was described by regional and international observers as largely peaceful, but they raised concerns about late electoral reforms, media freedom and access to the media in the run-up to the poll. The EU observation mission said restrictions on the opposition may have contributed to an "uneven contest". On vote tallying, the mission described a heavy military presence as intimidating and said it had received reports of attacks on some tallying centres. It said staff in many centres did not record results on tally sheets as soon as they were announced, and cited weak verification between digital entries and paper records. It added that returning officers frequently paused proceedings while awaiting instructions from headquarters. item.title: Four arrested over suspected poisoning of elephants in Kenya
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c790w8wxv0do?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Four arrested over suspected poisoning of elephants in Kenya - Published Four people have been arrested in Kenya as part of an investigation into a spate of mysterious elephant deaths over the past two months, officials have said. Three Kenyans and one Tanzanian have been detained on suspicion of poisoning at least 18 elephants in the Amboseli National Park, the Kenya Wildlife Service told the BBC. The investigation is looking into whether the elephants died from cyanide poisoning after eating large quantities of tomatoes sprayed with illegal pesticides. Preliminary laboratory tests have found traces of cyanide in samples of the crops taken from the elephants' stomachs. All of the affected elephants - mainly female adults and their calves - had also shown signs of paralysis, which authorities believe also points to cyanide poisoning. Tomato farms are found in the Kimana area, which is part of a corridor between Amboseli National Park and the Tsavo National Park in southern Kenya. It is a vast area known as the Amboseli ecosystem, which straddles the border near Tanzania where more than 2,000 elephants move along in search of food and water. Pesticides prohibited in Kenya are sometimes smuggled across this porous border with Tanzania and used in farms within the Amboseli area, where elephants live near human settlements and are known to raid farms for food. While regulations against illegal agrochemicals exist, there is weak enforcement and little attention paid to how they can affect animals. The suspects have been released on bail and the investigation continues.

item.title: China probes use of formaldehyde to keep cabbages fresh
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy9ze48l2yeo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
China probes use of formaldehyde to keep cabbages fresh - Published Authorities in China have launched an investigation into reports of formaldehyde being used to preserve the freshness of cabbages for human consumption. Officials in the north-eastern Hebei province confirmed that they had verified footage showing individuals dipping cabbages in a solution before loading them onto trucks for transportation. An environmental blogger first released the footage last week. Using formaldehyde, a colourless chemical used for preserving biological specimens that is known to cause cancer, for keeping food fresh is strictly prohibited in China. China is the world's largest producer of cabbages, most of which are exported to neighbouring countries in Asia. Police have taken legal action against the individuals involved, according to state media. Officials are now moving swiftly to prevent panic and restore confidence by carrying out spot checks on markets across the country. Chinese state media says investigators will also establish how widespread the practice is and take measures to trace affected vegetables. Local authorities in Kangbao county said in a statement issued on Saturday: "Any illegal or non-compliant practices discovered will be dealt with strictly in accordance with the law to ensure the safety of the vegetable supply." Xinfadi market in Beijing, one of the major sources of fresh produce in the capital, issued a statement saying that it had investigated the source of its cabbages, adding that none of the affected vegetables had entered its market. The incident has generated widespread media attention in China. An editorial in the People's Daily wrote: "The wholesalers focused solely on their immediate economic interests while completely disregarding the lives and health of consumers. [They] crossed a legal red line and breached the moral bottom line." China produces well over 30 million tonnes of cabbages each year, nearly half of the world's annual total. Vietnam, South Korea and Russia are among the largest export destinations for the vegetable. Exposure to relatively high quantities of formaldehyde in some workplaces has been linked to some types of cancer in humans, but the effect of exposure to small amounts is less clear, according to the American Cancer Society.

item.title: New Zealand to introduce bill for under-16s social media ban
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj068q7qj19o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
New Zealand to introduce bill for under-16s social media ban - Published New Zealand is to introduce a bill seeking to ban under-16s from using social media. Under the latest proposals, platforms including TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat and Facebook, will have to take steps to check users are over 16 and platforms that fail to meet their obligations could face fines of up to 10% of their global revenue. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said social media was exposing children to "harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not equipped to deal with". But several political parties have said they will vote against the bill. The move follows a similar ban in Australia, while countries including the UK and Greece are set to introduce restrictions next year. Luxon said social media was affecting children's family life, mental health, sleep and education. "We have protections to keep children safe in the real world and we need them in the virtual world too," he said. New Zealand's government has not outlined which other "high risk" platforms could be impacted. A statement said that under the Online Safety Bill, which is being introduced to parliament on Monday, social media companies would be required to "take reasonable steps" to check users are over the age of 16 by using methods including existing account information, facial age estimation and digital identity checks. Platforms regularly used by children would also be required to regularly assess the risks they pose and report on how they are being identified and reduced. No penalties are proposed for children, parents or caregivers for breaches of the ban, but fines for social media companies could be substantially higher than in Australia, where the maximum penalty is $99m (£51.7m). - Under-16s will be banned from social media from early 2027 - Published15 June - France's top court blocks social media ban for under-15s - Published14 August It is unclear if the bill will get enough votes to pass however, after both the Act and New Zealand First (NZF) parties - which are coalition partners in the government - said they would oppose it. David Seymour, New Zealand's deputy prime minister and leader of Act, said the ban would not work. Foreign affairs minister Winston Peters, who leads the NZF party, said: "We have been concerned with the proposed legislation and the direction and slippery slope that legislation like this will inevitably take our country." Peters also described a ban introduced in Australia in December as a "colossal failure". The ban has been difficult for Australia to enforce, and it has been widely acknowledged that many children under the age of 16 have still been able to access and use banned apps. Earlier this month, France's top court struck down a similar proposed social media ban, saying it infringed upon freedom of expression. Related topics - Published2 days ago - Published5 days ago

item.title: Guinea rubbish landfill collapse kills 31
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4g3g36z7p6o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Guinea rubbish landfill collapse kills 31 - Published At least 31 people have been killed after a mound of rubbish at a major waste site collapsed onto nearby homes in Guinea's capital Conakry, the government has said. Another 22 people were injured, including six seriously, in the city's Dar-es-Salam area. "Significant" resources and personnel - including the military - were deployed to search for survivors after the collapse at about 02:00 local time following heavy rain overnight, the government added in a statement. One woman told local media her five children had died in the disaster. There are fears that the death toll will rise further. Rescuers were later seen using excavators to comb through a mountain of scattered rubbish at the site as local residents gathered nearby. One eyewitness said many people were buried when a second part of the site gave way. "People tried to come to the rescue [after the first section collapsed]... They came running and climbed onto the refuse to see if anyone was there," Robert Kamano Sâa told the Associated Press. "That was when the second section collapsed in three successive stages, cascading down. And that is what poured onto the people." Guinea's Prime Minister Mamadou Oury Bah has visited the scene to assess the situation and oversee the search efforts. Mamadouba Bangoura, who lost his house in the collapse, said he and his family were woken up by the "loud noise" of the first wave of rubbish, which did not reach them. "[Then] the second wave came. That is what knocked over - pushed the house - and it fell," he told Reuters news agency. "There were a lot of people [buried]... It is very, very difficult to talk about it because seeing a human being lose their life like that is pathetic, it is so painful." Neighbourhood leader Lancine Sylla had earlier told the AFP news agency that he feared there would be a heavy death toll. "We have pulled out 18 bodies that were taken to the morgue," he said. Visiting the injured in hospital, Health Minister Khaïté Sall said they would get free medical care, while assuring families of government support. Guinea has experienced similar landslide tragedies before, with 10 people being killed at the same site in 2017. The government had recently ordered people living close to the site to move, but many residents chose to stay. Guinea's opposition figure and former Prime Minister Cellou Dalein Diallo, who is in exile abroad, called the accident "a tragedy that plunges us into dismay". "This tragedy is all the more worrying because the closure of the landfill had been announced for this Sunday, 23 August", he said. Rescue teams are continuing to search through the waste for others trapped underneath. Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent. item.title: Four arrested over boxing champion's murder in South Africa
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg7k9rmnzp7o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Four arrested over boxing champion's murder in South Africa - Published Four people have been arrested in South Africa in connection with the murder of boxing champion Zolani Tete, who was shot dead outside his home on Friday. Tete, 38, was gunned down in what has been described as an ambush in Mdantsane, Eastern Cape. A young woman who was with him was also shot and is in hospital. One of the men being held, a 22-year-old who was arrested on Saturday, will make an initial appearance in court on Monday, and faces murder and attempted murder charges. Tete held the WBO bantamweight title from 2017 to 2019, as well as the IBF super-flyweight title in 2014. He was later given a four-year ban, which lapsed in July this year. The remaining suspects, who were arrested on Sunday, are due in court on Tuesday. Two have been charged with unlawful possession of firearms and ammunition. It is unclear whether they will also be charged with murder and attempted murder. Tete was in his car waiting for the gate to his house to open when two armed suspects in balaclavas emerged from a vehicle and fired "multiple shots" at him and a 27‑year‑old female passenger, according to officials. The motive behind the attack is unclear. Tributes have been pouring in for the two-time world champion since his death. South Africa's Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie said: "South Africa has lost one of the finest fighters it has ever produced." Former Sports Minister Fikile Mbalula also paid tribute to Tete, lamenting the loss of a "a great South African who has made an immense contribution in the sport of boxing". Tete beat Liverpool's Paul Butler in 2015 in one of the eight times he fought in the United Kingdom. He also holds a Guinness World Record for the fastest knockout in a title fight, ending his match with Siboniso Gonya inside 11 seconds in 2017. Tete last fought in July 2022, beating Briton Jason Cunningham by knockout In London, but it was later ruled a no-contest after he failed a drugs test. He tested positive for anabolic steroid stanozolol and was given a ban by the UK Anti-Doping Agency. After his death, manager Mla Tengimfene confirmed he had been training for a comeback fight after his ban ended. Tete had 29 wins in 34 fights, with four losses and one no-contest. South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world. According to the latest crime statistics, covering the period between January and March this year, around 58 people were killed each day. item.title: Maradona's 'Hand of God' ball sells for £2.5m
item.description:

========================================
Maradona's 'Hand of God' ball sells for £2.5m - Published The football with which Diego Maradona scored his famous 'hand of God' goal at the 1986 World Cup has sold at auction for £2.5m. Maradona famously punched the ball past goalkeeper Peter Shilton in Argentina's 2-1 quarter-final win over England. After the game, he told reporters it had been scored "a little with the head of Maradona and a little with the hand of God". Maradona later scored what became known as the 'goal of the century' in the same game, dribbling past five England outfield players before slotting the ball past Shilton. Though it sold for $3.3m (£2.5m) at Heritage Auctions in the United States on Saturday, the ball had been expected to fetch nearer $10m (£7.3m). Speaking to Reuters before the auction, Mike Provenzale, a specialist auctioneer at Heritage, said: "It's a true one-of-one item. Arguably the most significant soccer item that exists." Tunisian Ali Bin Nasser, who refereed the match in 1986, collected the Adidas Azteca ball at full-time and kept it for more than three decades. In 2023, he signed a letter to confirm it was the only ball used during the match, which has also been confirmed by further independent authentication. Bin Nasser sold the ball in 2022 for $2.37m (£1.74m). Its new owner again put it up for auction in 2023 though it did not sell as bids did not meet the minimum value set. The shirt worn by Maradona during the same match sold for £7.1m at auction in 2022. Related topics - Published8 June - Published8 June

item.title: Ex-cricket captains urge 'proper medical care' for Imran Khan
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2z889l0dxo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Ex-cricket captains urge 'proper medical care' for Imran Khan - Published A group of former cricket captains, including Indian batting legend Sunil Gavaskar and one of England's longest-serving skippers Sir Alastair Cook, have called on Pakistan to ensure its ex-PM Imran Khan be given proper care while in custody. The cricketer-turned-politician has been in jail since 2023 on corruption charges which he denies. In a letter to Pakistan's current leader Shehbaz Sharif, the 21 former skippers aired concern that Khan, 73, was allowed "only a few hours" at a hospital last week where he was examined by a state-appointed team. Khan's party has also filed a contempt petition against the government for not giving him access to his own doctors, as ordered by the top court. The former cricket captains laid out three demands in their letter, the first of which is that Khan be assessed by a medical board directed by Pakistan's Supreme Court – which would include his personal physicians – particularly on the reported loss of vision in his right eye. They also urged authorities to allow weekly visits by Khan's family, as ordered by the court, "without interruptions or administrative delays". Finally, they asked that any treatment recommended by the medical board be "provided without delay". "Imran Khan is 73 years old and has now spent more than three years in custody," read the letter initiated by former Australian captain Greg Chappell. "Whatever the legal and political arguments surrounding his case, the basic decency of ensuring a court-ordered medical process is actually completed is not, in our view, a controversial request." Among the other signatories were England's Michael Atherton, Michael Brearley, Nasser Hussain, Andrew Strauss and David Gower, India's Kapil Dev and Dilip Vengsarkar, and Australia's Belinda Clark, Adam Gilchrist, Steve Waugh and Kim Hughes. Fourteen of the former skippers had also supported an earlier appeal for "humane treatment and proper medical care" for Khan which was submitted in February. Khan's lawyer claimed at the time that his client had 15% vision left in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action. The signatories of both letters had described themselves as "former colleagues and rivals who share a bond forged on the cricket field", adding that the bond "transcends the borders and disputes that too often divide countries". Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022. He was imprisoned in August 2023 and has faced charges in more than 100 cases, ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts, all of which he and his party Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf say are politically motivated. His jailing sparked large-scale protests by supporters, which were met with a crackdown by authorities. Pakistan's Supreme Court had on Tuesday directed the government to transfer Khan to a private hospital to be examined by physicians. He was instead seen by doctors at a government-run hospital in Islamabad, who deemed him "medically fit", before he was moved back to prison.

item.title: Trump says Canada wants 'benefits' of being US state after trade talks collapse
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx272np7vgyo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Trump says Canada wants 'benefits' of being US state after trade talks collapse - Published US President Donald Trump has said Canada wants "the benefits of being a state, without being one" after trade talks between the two countries collapsed late on Friday. The breakdown of negotiations triggered new 50% US tariffs on a range of Canadian goods. Trump also said American farmers had been charged "massive amounts of Tariffs" for years. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called the fresh tariffs a "miscalculation" designed to "hurt and divide us". Carney confirmed he would match Trump's tariffs "dollar-for-dollar" from 8 September, including levies on steel, dairy, appliances and electronics, saying the US and Canada were now in a trade war. Both countries were optimistic of a deal earlier in the week, but talks fell apart after both sides accused the other of making last-minute changes. "They asked too much and they offered too little," Carney said on Saturday. "You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked." Trump's latest comments echo his repeated references to making Canada the "51st state" of America since returning to office, sparking frustration among its leaders and residents. The collapse of the trade talks upended a deeply integrated trading relationship with no clear path to resolution. "We cannot accept what they've offered and we will not give what they've asked," Carney said. Trump told Fox News on Sunday that the Canadians were "foolish" to engage in a trade war with the US and think they will "actually win". The new 50% US tariffs will apply to a range of Canadian goods, in addition to existing US tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminium, automobiles and lumber. They are limited in scope, covering about $20bn (£15bn; C$28bn) of imports from Canada, or about 5% in total, including wine, dairy, cement, clothing and hockey equipment. The prime minister said Canada was retaliating "reluctantly" to protect its interests, with details of counter-measures to be released in the coming days. - Carney faces crucial test after walking away from Trump's deal - Published1 day ago Leaders of other federal parties in Canada, including the Conservative opposition, voiced support for the prime minister, as have the leaders of some Canadian provinces. Tariffs - a tax on goods imported from other countries - have been a key component of Trump's trade policy, with the US president arguing that they will boost American manufacturing and create jobs at home. Critics, however, say tariffs have raised prices for American consumers, and have disrupted and damaged the global economy. Carney's speech on Saturday was his first address to Canadians after he announced late on Friday night that a deal would not be reached, accusing the US side of making "last-minute changes" that were "unfair" and "uneconomic". US negotiators, meanwhile, accused Canada of making "new demands and walk backs" on terms which had been previously agreed. US trade representative Jamieson Greer told Fox News on Saturday that there were no plans to resume talks. He added that the US had been prepared to cut some of its tariffs on Canada as part of the ill-fated deal. Carney, however, said the US presented "unacceptable" terms that were too restrictive, including curbing Canada's ability to strike new trade deals with other countries. He also rejected the assertion that Canada had made last-minute requests: "We clarified what was on offer and were continually disappointed by the answers." Doug Ford, the leader of Canada's most populous province Ontario, backed Carney and said Trump "can't be trusted". British Columbia Premier David Eby said the US demand for restrictions on Canada's ability to have other trade deals "would reduce us to the economic equivalent of the 51st state". "It was never acceptable to Canadians," Eby said. The Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre also appeared to support Carney, calling the latest US levies "unjustified". Quebec's premier, Christine Fréchette, warned jobs would likely be lost as a result of the new US tariffs. "Behind these numbers are real people," she said, vowing to introduce measures to support impacted sectors. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, whose oil-rich province has worked to make inroads with the Trump administration, urged both sides to resume talks. The collapse comes after more than a year of on-again, off-again trade talks, which intensified in recent weeks after a US-imposed deadline to strike a deal or face further tariffs. The two countries were also engaged in a mandatory review of an existing North American free trade agreement, known as USMCA, with Mexico. The pact was signed by Trump during his first term to replace the 1994 North American Free Trade Agreement. It underpins $1.6tn (£1.2tn) in annual trilateral trade across Canada, the US and Mexico. Earlier this summer, Canada and Mexico had formally requested for USMCA to be renewed for another 16 years. The US, however, declined to renew it in its current form. Asked how Friday's trade talk collapse would impact the North American free trade pact, Carney said it was "certainly not good news".

item.title: Divorce, smartphones and control - BBC sees how Taliban run Afghanistan
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgvk9p2n7ko?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Divorce, smartphones and control - BBC sees how Taliban run Afghanistan - Published Governor Abdullah Sarhadi gives money to treat a boy's broken arm and hands out funds for a local mosque - then, in his office in northern Afghanistan, an astonishing exchange unfolds. A young woman tells the grey-bearded former Taliban commander that she wants to divorce her husband, who she accuses of months of abuse and beatings. She will not take no for an answer. In a country where girls are banned from secondary education, the 18-year-old argues her case calmly and confidently, her face completely hidden behind a full-face veil and sunglasses. "If there was any chance to live together, I wouldn't be here… I have taken my decision," she says. After trying to persuade her to avoid divorce, the governor later comments that women are "mindless" and "deficient in intellect", to laughter from the male officials, bodyguards and elders around him. The moment gives a rare glimpse into the day-to-day realities of the Taliban's rule, five years after they swept aside the US-backed government in 2021. In that time, women have been excluded from most workplaces, banned from universities and may not travel alone or visit parks and leisure centres. In encounters spread over two years, the BBC gained unusual access to influential figures in the extreme Islamist movement, spending time with men who once planned suicide attacks or spent years in underground hideouts, but are now officials and soldiers. The Taliban came into power saying they had changed, but many of their policies are similar to the hard-line interpretation of Sharia - Islamic religious law - they imposed in the 1990s. The men we met seemed to want to present themselves as reasonable, yet were not keen to discuss their past violence. And we saw moments of unease between the rulers and those they rule. Governor Sarhadi says Tuba – not her real name – should stay in the marriage. "Ask yourself: 'Who would marry me after I get my divorce?'" says Sarhadi. "You'll have to compromise a lot or you'll lose your dignity and honour." "Mr Governor, my honour and dignity have already been ruined," she responds. Her husband listens, awaiting his turn to speak. Under Sharia, a woman requesting that her husband agrees to a divorce may have to return some or all of the money given to her by him when they married. A financial settlement is often agreed. But this woman's husband says he wants four times the amount, which her family refuses to pay. The governor says the woman should be given her own room. He adds that officials will warn him not to beat her - "otherwise he'd be jailed". Unsatisfied, Tuba's father later tells the BBC the family will pursue divorce through the courts, even though, under the Taliban's court system, it is very difficult for a woman to get a divorce without the husband's consent. Sarhadi was a military commander during the Taliban's first stint in power in the 1990s. He was among thousands of insurgents who surrendered in late 2001 as a US-led coalition ousted the group. He was held for several years in US detention in Guantanamo Bay, but eventually released. When the Taliban regained power, he became a governor - first in the province of Bamiyan, then when we met him in late June, in Sheberghan city in Jawzjan province. He has recently become deputy commander of a military corps in the northern province of Kunduz. Tapping on an old-style mobile with a tiny screen, he says a recent ban on smartphones for officials has slowed things down. "Before, you could send a quick message… sending documents and getting an answer fast." If he says any more about the ban, "it will cause trouble", he adds. But in other ways his worldview seems largely unchanged from the Taliban's position 25 years ago. Then, he was a military commander in Bamiyan, where the Taliban blew up ancient giant Buddha statues, triggering international shock and condemnation. He initially tries to avoid our questions about the archaeological site, but eventually, he says: "I destroyed it with my own hands. "Whatever we did and we do is in accordance with the guidance and God's law… We smash idols rather than sell them. Why should I regret? It was God's will." In the capital Kabul, we meet another senior Taliban figure who swapped a violent past for a role with the ruling administration. Habibullah Badr drives us through the streets in an armoured car. He says he was previously "responsible for the operations of suicide attackers" in Kabul. "I know all the roads and streets very well… we had all the information we needed about Kabul and its alleys," he says. "There were areas that needed a long time to plan." Taliban suicide attacks killed thousands of people in Afghanistan, including many civilians. Badr is cautious about discussing his past though, fearing it will "make people upset" and could "reopen wounds". Asked about civilian deaths, he says the Taliban targeted US convoys and that civilians were urged to stay away from foreign bases. Whenever I try to ask him about specific attacks that took place in civilian areas, he evades the question. He is currently taking time out from official roles for medical treatment, but was previously deputy head of prisons for the whole country – and ran the very jail where he was held on death row under the previous government. Badr invites us to join him at a tribal gathering, where the head of a charitable foundation is to honour him with a medal. But things take an unexpected turn. "Mr Badr is a pride for Afghanistan and a great fighter," says Sultan Mohammad Talaee. "But I also have a complaint. If the schools and education were open to all it would be a great work for Afghanistan. I hope this doesn't offend you." An awkward silence follows, his audience unsure how to react. Talaee's microphone is swiftly removed. Afterwards, he tells the BBC: "I requested for the girls' schools to reopen… seeking knowledge is an obligation for both men and women in Islam." He adds: "There were other things I wanted to say but they didn't let me talk more." The Taliban: Coming Out of the Shadows Audiences in the UK can watch on iPlayer from 17:00 and on Global Eye on BBC Two at 19:00 Often those who speak out face much more severe consequences. Women told us of the deep despair they felt over dreams thwarted by restrictions on education, and of friends jailed for protesting. Most journalists we spoke to said they had been summoned or questioned by the Taliban's intelligence organisation, Estikhbaraat. The BBC put some of these concerns to the Taliban government's spokesman, known as Zabihullah Mujahid. He has been a public face for the Taliban government since 2021. He still uses the pseudonym he went by for years during the insurgency, but he told us his real name is Tahir Shah Seddiqi - revealing it publicly for the first time. In a lavish press centre funded by the Americans for the previous government, we ask him about the first press conference he gave there, two days after the Taliban took control of the country. Then, he told the world the Taliban government would allow women to work and study "within our frameworks" and they would "be very active" in society. Why did they fail to keep their word? "We are committed to women's rights, freedom of speech and other things within Sharia," he replies. "We should see everything through the Sharia lens." Allowing women to work in offices such as his own "would lead to immoralities" and "their dignity would be undermined", he adds. He says the issue of education for women is "under discussions… we need a Sharia-based solution for it". When questioned about the Taliban's crackdown on media freedom, he says: "In a society like Afghanistan we have our restrictions. We can't let media do whatever propaganda they want… they can't broadcast against Islamic laws and rites." The Taliban government sits in Kabul, but Mujahid spends a lot of time in the southern city of Kandahar, the Taliban's heartland, which some now consider the de facto capital. We ask to meet the Taliban's supreme leader, Hibatullah Akhundzada, who is based there. He rarely appears in public and has never given a media interview - we are told it will not be possible at the moment. Restrictions have been tightened in Kandahar since I last visited two years ago. Now men must have beards. Radio stations are not allowed to play music or broadcast women's voices, and we were not allowed to film in the city. Two hours' drive away, along dusty roads, some of the group's most devoted former fighters showed the BBC the insurgents' old secret cave network. Abid Lalai, a former fighter who now mans a checkpoint as part of a security force under the interior ministry, shows us the holes he fired from and the places he used to put his Quran and hang AK-47s. His superior, Abdul Samad, shows us an unmarked graveyard, saying his father is buried here, killed fighting for the Taliban. The area is one of the most deprived in a country where the UN says three in four people cannot provide for their basic needs. Samad says the local population desperately need water, roads and clinics. "Emirate [Taliban] officials have not forgotten us," says Samad. He says the leaders may be busy with other priorities. "We are hopeful, they will look after us sometime." Five years since the Taliban began their second stint in power, poverty, unemployment and economic instability remain pressing concerns. Taliban figures we spoke to said they were working to tackle them, but we met other people who believe the group itself is the country's main problem. "I'm speechless about how a group that has no understanding about life is suddenly in power," says Hoda - not her real name - a woman who protested on the streets when the Taliban first returned to power. "Women can't accept this situation," she tells the BBC. "They might advance restrictions but it won't stay like this forever." "I think the Taliban are scared of educated women," she adds. "That's why they restrict women. They want uneducated women so they can't raise wise men. Because that would end the Taliban." Additional reporting by Hafizullah Maroof

item.title: 'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade war
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy0j0zz8l83o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade war - Published Cindy Baldassi relies on American buyers to keep her stone-and-glass jewellery company going. Some 75% of sales of pieces including amethyst, sea glass and agates from her business, CindyLouWho2, based in Calgary, Alberta, come from Americans. But after trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed over the weekend and leaders of both countries pledged to slap 50% tariffs on each other's products, business owners on both sides of the border are bracing for the fallout. With a majority of the items she sells falling under US President Donald Trump's newly imposed tariffs, Baldassi says she will need to add 50% to the price of most of her products to stay afloat. "It's quite likely that it will wipe out most of my US sales," Baldassi told the BBC. "I expect that at least half of my business will be gone." Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has pledged levies starting on 8 September on US steel, dairy, appliances and electronics. Trump tariffs went into effect on Saturday, hitting Canadian wine, dairy, cement, clothing and hockey equipment. 'We may get killed' In Canada, it is not clear how much more severe the impacts will be, since the country has grown somewhat used to the on-again-off-again trade war. Lind Furniture has been in business for almost 60 years in the Canadian province of Ontario, selling leather furniture to big store clients like Sears and Costco over the years. Sales dropped when Trump took office in 2025. "As soon as there were tariffs in the air, people put purchases on hold," Michael Saifer, general manager of Lind Furniture, told the BBC. - Trump says Canada wants 'benefits' of being US state after trade talks collapse - Published23 hours ago Now, his concern centres around Canadians' chances for victory. "Everyone wants to sell to the Americans - they can buy from whoever they want," he said. "I don't know that we're going to win a war with them; we may get killed." The US tariffs that took effect after talks broke off on Friday apply to about $20bn (£15bn; C$28bn) worth of Canadian exports to the US - about 5% of what Canada ships to the US annually. The levies add to US tariffs already in place on Canadian steel, aluminium, automobiles and lumber. Canada would be very exposed if the import taxes multiply on both sides because 70% of its exports are to the US. Navigating what comes next as both sides are dug in is proving a delicate balance for some business owners. Like many retailers, Matteo Sgaramella, founder of Toronto-based menswear brand Outclass, told the BBC that his company collects orders from clothing designers months before they are due to arrive in stores. Products that US stores ordered in January will arrive in September but now with a new tariff. "If I contact them now and tell them, hey, you know, you may get an extra 50% bill from UPS on top of what you need to pay me for this shipment, they're all going to say, 'no way, don't ship it,'" Sgaramella said. He still has to figure out where that additional cost will go. "There's going to be a lot of people that go out of business because of this," Sgaramella said, but noted that only 20% of his wholesale sales and 20% of his e-commerce come from the US. "Big business can, you know, always find a way... but small businesses are going to get smashed by this." 'It's going to get worse before it gets better' The impacts are not only being felt north of the US-Canada border. Carney promised his tariffs hitting US products in September will match Trump's "dollar-for-dollar". Details of the countermeasures will be released in the coming days, he said. For Mike Roach and Kim Osgood, owners of Paloma Clothing, a clothing store in Portland, Oregon, that means preparing for one of their best-selling items to potentially increase sizably in price. Osgood creates designs that she has a Montreal-based company transfer onto pillows the couple sells in their store. Those pillows are their best-selling gift item, retailing at $59. With the newly imposed tariffs, a normal markup would bring the price of that pillow to somewhere between $86 and $90, Osgood told the BBC. "Gift items are really price-point sensitive; people have in their mind what they're going to pay for a gift, and they're not going to pay more than that," Roach said. The couple, whose shop has been operating for 51 years, say they will likely hold the original price and hope the "tariff problem," as Roach calls it, gets worked out. "It would be one thing if we had three months' notice; that would be something you could plan around, do some work with the vendors, but when it happens literally overnight you're really stuck," he said. While the tariffs could mean changes for the Paloma Clothing company, other American companies are facing the same battle they have faced since Trump returned to office and began imposing his levies. Bill Easton, owner of Terre Rouge Wines in Plymouth, California, has been unable to ship his wine north to Canada for the past year and a half due to a boycott of US alcohol. He is currently paying $2,400 a month to store that wine in a warehouse in the hope that he will one day be able to ship it to the Canadian markets he sells to. "The wine has just gotten better in the warehouse, but I can't expect my customer in Canada to pay that extra cost that I've assumed over the last year and a half as part of the price, if I was able to sell it tomorrow," Easton told the BBC. And then there are the American businesses impacted by proximity to the Canadian border. The number of Canadian customers travelling across the border to shop at Heather Seevers' craft shop, Northwest Yarns and Mercantile in Bellingham, Washington, has gone down some 20% since the tariff war began over a year ago. What has further irked Canadians has been Trump musing on Canada becoming a 51st US state. The shop sits 25 minutes from the US-Canada border and since the "war" ensued Seevers said her business received emails from Canadian customers saying they could not patronise her business "due to anti-Canadian rhetoric". "We completely understood that," she said. But the combined impact of fewer customers and higher prices has left the shop asking for help from the community recently via a fundraising initiative to stay afloat. And then, over the weekend, when the new tariffs struck, Seevers saw another hurdle appear. "It's going to get worse before it gets better," she said. "It's going to take years and years and years to get a relationship back with Canada, and I think these new tariffs are digging us deeper into a hole." item.title: Australian shark attack victim grateful for 'second chance at life'
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c87n792dnlno?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Australian shark attack victim grateful for 'second chance at life' - Published An Australian woman bitten by a shark at a popular Sydney beach earlier this year says she has been given a "second chance at life" and will be making the most of it. Leah Stewart, 34, was mauled by a shark during a morning swim at Coogee Beach in June, suffering multiple bites to her arms and legs, amid a spate of attacks in Australia. The mother-of-one was placed in an induced coma and had several surgeries, including having one of her arms amputated. In an online post on Monday, she thanked her supporters who have raised more than AU$550,000 (US$394,000; £289,000) for her, saying her recovery has been "incredibly difficult" but she is making "remarkable" progress. "After what has been an incredibly difficult few months, I'm so happy that I've progressed enough to build some independence, and I can finally see some light after all of this," Stewart wrote, in her first comments since the attack. "I want you to know that I feel like I've been given a second chance at life, and I'm not going to waste it." Stewart said she had been "overwhelmed" by the support from family, friends and "even strangers", adding that the "you've inspired me to get better, not bitter". An online fundraiser for her would now be closed, she wrote, with the money raised giving her the chance to recover at home as well as "options for further medical treatment down the road". "I still have a long way to go, but my recovery has been remarkable, and a huge part of that is because of the absolute army of love, support, prayers and encouragement surrounding my family and I from all over the world." In an interview with Nine Network's 60 Minutes, due to be aired this weekend, Stewart described seeing the shark's "horrific" face. "I'll never forget its face - it was a monster," she says. "It was holding onto my leg and I just thought of (my daughter) August, and I thought, 'she's not going to have a mum. She's gonna grow up without a mum'." Fighting back tears, she goes on: "I couldn't handle that, I didn't want her to not have a mum. I just thought, I've got to fight it, do everything I can to be here." There have been a spate of shark attacks in Australia this year, with four attacks over a two-day period in January, including one on a 12-year-old boy who later died from his injuries. In May, a man was killed by a shark in Queensland while spearfishing and in Western Australia, a father-of-two died after he was attacked by a 4m (13ft) shark.
